description: We are a data-driven team aiming to win the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our project, CLPS Lunar Mission Browser, turns complex lunar mission data into actionable insights. We seek teammates skilled in Python, data analysis, visualization, web development, or space science. We value rigorous reasoning, technical excellence, creativity and ownership. Our goal is to build a scientifically grounded, intuitive tool that stands out for its insight and execution. We are here to compete for the top spot.
summary: VNI Moon Navigator is an interactive 3D web app for exploring and comparing lunar landing sites over time. Select a site to view its location, terrain-derived horizon, and the changing positions of the Sun and Earth. A time control visualizes sunlight and geometric Earth-visibility windows. The app combines NASA’s LOLA elevation data with JPL Horizons calculations, while showing sources, assumptions, and limitations. Its AI assistant explains the app’s calculated results and helps compare sites using the same underlying data. By making lunar terrain and lighting conditions easier to understand, VNI Moon Navigator helps mission planners, educators, and the public explore how location and timing affect solar power potential and direct-to-Earth visibility. It is a decision-support and educational tool, not a guarantee of landing safety or radio communication.
details:
Project Overview

VNI Moon Navigator is an interactive web application for exploring lunar landing sites and understanding how location and time affect surface conditions. It brings lunar terrain data and astronomical calculations into one visual interface, helping students, educators, and mission-planning enthusiasts explore questions that are difficult to answer using separate scientific tools.

How It Works

Users explore a 3D Moon, select a source-verified landing site, and choose the present time or another date and time. Selecting a site opens a concise information card; a detailed panel then presents the location’s coordinates, terrain and sky information, calculated measurements, data sources, and limitations.

The application uses elevation data from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) to model the local terrain horizon. It compares the terrain-aware horizon with a smooth-Moon baseline to show how nearby and distant terrain can affect whether the Sun or Earth is visible. Data from JPL Horizons provides the Sun’s and Earth’s apparent directions and elevations for the selected site and time. Users can explore these values over time, view illumination changes, examine horizon visualizations, and compare sites.

The 3D scene also provides simple visual indicators for the Sun and Earth to help users understand their directions relative to the Moon. Their displayed sizes and distances are illustrative and are not to scale. Measurements and scientific conclusions are kept distinct from visual effects.

AI Assistant

The application includes an optional AI assistant that can explain displayed results and help users compare locations. The assistant uses the application’s structured calculation results rather than independently inventing measurements. Users provide their own Anthropic API key through the app; the key is not included in the project code. The application checks numerical claims in AI responses against the values returned by its calculation tools.

Data, Technology, and Validation

The app is built as a browser-based application using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js-based 3D rendering. Its scientific data and sources are organized in the project, and precomputed ephemeris data allow the core visualization to work without making a live JPL Horizons request for every interaction.

The team validates data coverage, coordinate conventions, units, and calculations against authoritative sources and comparison checks. Results are presented with their sources, assumptions, and known limitations.

Importance and Limitations

Understanding illumination and Earth visibility can help users compare lunar sites and dates, explore potential sunlight periods, and investigate geometric opportunities for direct-to-Earth visibility. This supports the challenge’s goal of making lunar site comparisons more intuitive and accessible.

The application is a research and educational decision-support tool. Earth appearing above the geometric horizon does not guarantee a working radio link, and the app does not certify that a location is safe or suitable for landing.

Use of AI Tools

AI tools assisted the team with research, planning, data analysis, writing, interface design, coding, debugging, and the development of the application’s AI assistant. The scientific source data come from NASA/JPL and other cited sources; AI-generated explanations do not replace the application’s calculations. The team reviews the project’s data, methods, and output.
